record.paper_title: Measurement of Energy Spectrum and Elemental Composition of PeV Cosmic Rays: Open Problems and Prospects
record.original_question: For very-high-energy γ-ray sources, how can observations determine whether the γ-rays are produced by π^0 decay in hadronic cosmic-ray interactions or instead by relativistic electrons through inverse Compton scattering or bremsstrahlung, so that PeV cosmic-ray source candidates can be identified conclusively?

evidence.quote: Unlike neutrinos that are produced only in hadronic interactions of CRs, the question whether the observed γ-rays are produced by the decay of π0 from CR interactions (‘hadronic’ mechanism), or by a population of relativistic electrons via Inverse Compton scattering or bremsstrahlung (‘leptonic’ mechanism), still needs a conclusive answer.
Therefore, the quest for CR sources to be able to accelerate particles up to the PeV range in a multi-messenger approach requires the observation of the γ-ray sky above 100 TeV.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a very-high-energy astrophysical γ-ray source observed across a broad photon energy range (from GeV up to and beyond 100 TeV). The observed γ-ray emission can in principle be produced by two distinct physical mechanisms:

1. Hadronic mechanism: high-energy protons and nuclei (cosmic rays) interact with ambient matter or radiation fields, producing neutral pions π^0 whose decay yields a γ-ray spectrum characterized (in the source rest frame) by a symmetric peak around m_{π^0}/2 ≈ 67.5 MeV in an E^2 dN/dE representation and by a spectrum extending to very high energies reflecting the underlying cosmic-ray spectrum; this channel also necessarily produces a corresponding flux of high-energy neutrinos from charged pion decay.

2. Leptonic mechanism: a population of relativistic electrons radiates γ-rays through inverse Compton scattering on ambient photon fields (CMB, infrared, optical) and/or via bremsstrahlung on ambient gas, with a spectral shape determined by the electron distribution and target fields, and without an accompanying neutrino flux.

Problem: Devise an observational and analytical procedure — using broadband γ-ray spectral measurements (including the morphology of the spectrum near the π^0 decay feature and its behavior above 100 TeV), spatial morphology correlated with target gas or photon fields, multiwavelength data, and multi-messenger constraints from coincident high-energy neutrino observations — that can conclusively discriminate, for a given source, between a π^0-decay hadronic origin and a leptonic (inverse Compton plus bremsstrahlung) origin of the γ-ray emission. The procedure should be sufficient to identify with confidence which observed very-high-energy γ-ray sources are sites of hadronic cosmic-ray acceleration up to PeV energies (PeVatrons).
artifact.status_search_result: The hadronic-versus-leptonic discrimination problem for VHE γ-ray sources remains an active open question in high-energy astrophysics. While π^0-decay signatures have been established in some supernova remnants via the GeV "pion bump" (Ackermann et al. 2013) and LHAASO has detected sources emitting beyond 100 TeV, the general identification of Galactic PeVatrons is still unresolved as of 2024–2026, with multi-messenger neutrino observations (IceCube, KM3NeT) considered key but not yet conclusive for most sources.

status_evidence.title: LHAASO Galactic PeVatron sources
status_evidence.snippet: Detection of 12 ultra-high-energy γ-ray sources above 100 TeV; nature of PeVatron accelerators remains uncertain
status_evidence.claim: Identification of hadronic PeV cosmic-ray sources remains open.

status_evidence.title: Fermi-LAT detection of pion-decay signature in SNRs
status_evidence.snippet: Characteristic pion-decay feature detected in two SNRs, providing direct evidence of hadronic acceleration in those specific sources
status_evidence.claim: Hadronic origin can be established in select cases but not generally at PeV energies.
